Yara signatures ...................................................................................... 81 mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 4TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com EXECUTIVE SUMMARY At the end of 2015 we became aware of an unusual malware program, discovered in an attempted attack on a bank in Singapore. Analysis of the file attached to a spear-phishing email that had been sent to the bank revealed the\xc2 name of the malware: JSocket. Later on we found that this malware has many names: Adwind RAT (Remote Access Tool), AlienSpy, Frutas, jFrutas, Unrecom, Sockrat, JSocket, jRat. The rich features of the malware, including its ability to run on Windows, Mac OS and Linux, as well as the fact that it was not detected by any antivirus solution meant that it immediately got our attention. Adwind is a backdoor available for purchase. It\xe2\x80\x99s written purely in Java which makes it cross-platform. The backdoor component (called the server) can\xc2 run on Windows, Mac OS, Linux and Android platforms, providing capabilities for remote desktop control, data gathering, data exfiltration and lateral movement. While it is more often used by opportunistic attackers and distributed in\xc2 massive spam campaigns, there are cases where Adwind has been used in\xc2 targeted attacks. In August 2015, Adwind popped up in the news in connection with a cyber-espionage campaign against an Argentinian prosecutor who had been found dead in January 2015. Currently the malware is distributed via a software-as-a-service platform which is based on an online subscription model. This report overviews the\xc2 capabilities of the malware, describes its online platform and lists the\xc2 cyber-attacks where this malware was used. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= http://motherboard.vice.com/read/malware-hunter-finds-spyware-used-against-dead-argentine-prosecutor 5TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com THE HISTORY OF ADWIND Frutas RAT The story begins in January 2012. A user of the Spanish-speaking hacking forum \xe2\x80\x9cindetectables.net\xe2\x80\x9d (the majority of whose users come from Mexico and South America), going by the name of \xe2\x80\x9cadwind\xe2\x80\x9d, started a new thread about the development and testing of a new cross-platform RAT codenamed \xe2\x80\x9cFrutas\xe2\x80\x9d, which was fully implemented in Java. A week later, on 17th January, he announced the first release of the RAT. Its\xc2 development was rapid and in late February version 0.4 was released. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 6TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com We found some information about that early variant: Name: Seerver.jar Size: 24\xe2\x80\x99034 bytes MD5: ea68f5067c916ce6afd72aa72e89450d After that new versions were released every two months: Date Version Size MD5 20.02.2012 0.4 24034 ea68f5067c916ce6afd72aa72e89450d 26.03.2012 0.6 32523 aa647cc251c0d63170c79c6ea64ae62d 7.05.2012 0.7 28148 9d28cb35d6e16f7e3c5382bcd95b621b 5.07.2012 0.8 ? ? mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 7TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com The author announced the following functionality in version 0.8: + Check for open port [Beta] + No-IP updater + Check for internal and external IP + Get some dns ip (Check only port 80) + Supports Unicode + Now it will be able to update the server via URL (for future updates) + Option to download and run any file + Sceenshot capture via right click + FileManager works with file systems on Linux and Windows (e.g. Linux client and server in Windows) + We can now choose the time between each reconnection. This was the first but by no means the last \xe2\x80\x9crebranding\xe2\x80\x9d of this malware. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 12TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com The first variant of the Adwind RAT, version 1.0, seems to have been released in January 2013, just four months after the final release of Frutas 1.0. The Adwind RAT gained worldwide attention and quickly became one of the\xc2 favorite tools among Arabic-speaking hackers, mostly used in conjunction with the DarkComet RAT. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 13TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 14TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com The most popular version of Adwind was 2.0, released in May 2013. Version 3.0 was released in August 2013. The author created a new YouTube channel to announce the new release and host video tutorials. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 15TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Version 3.0 of the Adwind RAT added support for Android OS, and from that moment Adwind was truly cross-platform, supporting all major OS including mobile: Windows, Linux, Mac OSX, Android. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 16TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Adwind 3.0 also introduced a subscription model with different plans: In the summer of 2013, Adwind was also being used in targeted attacks around the world and, for the first time was seen in attacks in the Asia-Pacific region. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 17TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Kaspersky Security Network detected Adwind fewer than 2,000 times during 2013, but nearly 70% of all targets were located in just ten countries, with Arabic and Spanish-speaking countries at the top: UNRECOM A second rebranding of the RAT took place in November 2013. Shortly after that, on 12 November 2013, the same \xe2\x80\x9cfaria\xe2\x80\x9d released information about a new RAT codenamed UNRECOM. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 19TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 20TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com UNRECOM (or LustroSoft) also used a subscription based model with different plans: The individual nicknamed \xe2\x80\x9dfaria\xe2\x80\x9d used skype and gmail accounts which revealed a connection to the distribution of UNRECOM. Considering that he entered the scene as a person related to the distribution of Adwind, we\xc2 believe that he is probably a friend or partner of the original Adwind author. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 21TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com UNRECOM version 1.3 was cracked by hacker Boredliner (boredliner.wordpress.com) in February 2014 and released to the public. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 22TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com The same software cracker (\xe2\x80\x9cBoredliner\xe2\x80\x9d) released a cracked version of Adwind 3.0 in February 2014: Software protection was based on license number and hardware checks. One\xc2 of new features of this variant of Adwind was a commercial obfuscation tool known as Allatori which is used for Java bytecode obfuscation. To check the serial number, Adwind established a connection to adwind.com.mx, which had to be resolved to a hardcoded IP: 65.99.225.111 mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= http://www.allatori.com/features.html 23TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com This cracked version of Adwind 3.0 was the main and most widely used variant of Adwind in targeted attacks based on Adwind during 2014-2015. The next version of UNRECOM (2.0) was released in March 2014. By the summer of 2014 there were two Java-based RATs circulating in the cybercriminal world, based on the same source code \xe2\x80\x93 Adwind v.2/3 (cracked) and UNRECOM (with \xe2\x80\x9cnew owner\xe2\x80\x9d, also cracked). mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 24TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com AlienSpy Obviously, the availability of free, cracked variants of the RAT caused a decline in sales that disturbed the author (regardless of how he was connected to UNRECOM) and his response was the introduction of a\xc2 new\xc2 \xe2\x80\x9crebranded\xe2\x80\x9d RAT in September-October 2014: AlienSpy RAT. The first known and widely distributed versions were 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2, with\xc2 the\xc2 latest released in October 2014. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 25TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 26TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Some versions of AlienSpy were also cracked and used by cybercriminals, but,\xc2 as we explained earlier, most of them relied on free Adwind or UNRECOM. This and previous facts were the reason behind the increased number of targeted attacks using this RAT. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 27TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Targeted email sample (image courtesy of contagiodump) In April 2015, Fidelis published the first detailed report on AlienSpy, based on known cases from dozens of attacks against US companies. \xe2\x80\x9cFidelis researchers have observed AlienSpy being sold in the cyber- underground via a subscription model, with prices starting at $9.90 for 15-day use to $219.90 for an annual subscription. The subscription provides users with access to the malware\xe2\x80\x99s complete range of capabilities, including some newer techniques like sandbox detection, antivirus tool disablement, and Transport Layer Security (TLS) encryption-protected command-and-control capabilities.\xe2\x80\x9d If you compare the prices quoted for AlienSpy with those for UNRECOM, it appears that short-term subscriptions for the new \xe2\x80\x9cbrand\xe2\x80\x9d were cheaper (starting at just $9.90), but an annual subscription was more expensive ($219.9\xc2 vs $200 for unlimited use of UNRECOM). mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 28TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com The Fidelis report was focused on the last known variant of AlienSpy \xe2\x80\x93 version\xc2 5.1. Code analysis revealed a lot of functions from UNRECOM (meaning that it was based on this RAT, not Adwind). The authentication server for AlienSpy was located at alienspy.net, registered in June 2014. However, the domain was suspended by GoDaddy after the Fidelis report \xe2\x80\x93 and the business of the AlienSpy author was ruined again. After just two months, in June 2015, the fifth reincarnation of Frutas was born\xc2 \xe2\x80\x93 this time under the name it is still known by today: the \xe2\x80\x9cJSocket RAT\xe2\x80\x9d. THE LATEST REINCARNATION OF\xc2 THE MALWARE JSocket.org: malware-as-a-service JSocket.org is a website that implements a concept known as malware-as- a-service, which is a commercially available malware tool that can be used on\xc2 a subscription basis, and which includes basic technical support, additional paid components and modules, as well as accompanying services such as obfuscation to evade AV detection, a free VPN service for members with the\xc2 ability to map ports for incoming connections at the VPN termination point and free checks using tens of different AV engines. The project runs openly as if it were providing completely legitimate products and services for benign purposes. It uses common online marketing methods to advertise the capabilities of its malware and the various techniques available for stealing information. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 29TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com The website is hosted or proxied via 37.61.235.30, an IP that belongs to LayerIP UK, a mysterious hosting company for which we couldn\xe2\x80\x99t find a public website. Registration As of January 2016, JSocket registration is open to everyone. To register you have to provide a valid email address which will be validated after initial sign up. Some of the additional features, such as the VPN service and additional downloads are only available to registered users. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 30TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Online malware shop The users who successfully complete the registration process get access to the online shop where they may purchase a subscription plan for the JSocket RAT, and buy additional components and services. The author of the videos has the local time zone set to UTC-5. Profitability JSocket.org offers six types of memberships ranging from 15 days to a one year subscription term which cost from $25 USD to $300 USD respectively. In\xc2 December the website had more than 1,600 registered users. The\xc2 estimated annual revenue of this online project is about $200,000 USD. LATEST KNOWN ADWIND ATTACKS At the end of 2015, the Adwind RAT was used to attack banks outside of Singapore, such as the Ajman bank in the United Arab Emirates, Bangkok Bank, the IBC Bank (USA), the Nordic financial services group Nordea, headquartered in Sweden, and possibly Bank Negara Malaysia. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 34TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Another attack that was discovered via an Adwind email sample uploaded to\xc2 VirusTotal revealed an attempt to attack a major bank in Russia. Although the actor behind that attack seems unrelated to the original attack, the trend to target banks via direct emails to employees seems to be on the rise. An email sent to a major bank in the Russian Federation Adwind was used in another reported attack in November 2015, which\xc2 centred on a spear-phishing email campaign sent on behalf of the\xc2 UAE\xc2 Police Force and carrying a warning about a terror threat. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 35TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com We found another example of an \xe2\x80\x9con behalf of Police\xe2\x80\x9d attack, also in November but from the \xe2\x80\x9cCommissariat de Police\xe2\x80\x9d in Belgium. At the end 2015 we observed some attacks based on the theme of \xe2\x80\x9cshipping\xe2\x80\x9d instead of \xe2\x80\x9cmoney transfer\xe2\x80\x9d. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 36TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Adwind/JSocket was also used for non-financially motivated attacks: mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 37TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com Malware Hunter Finds Spyware Used Against Dead Argentine Prosecutor WRITTEN BY LORENZO FRANCESCHI-BICCHIERAI August 6, 2015 // 07:50 AM EST That name, \xe2\x80\x9cestrictamente secreto y confidencial.pdf.jar,\xe2\x80\x9d [strictly secret and confidential.pdf.jar] was enough to provide Marquis-Boire with a lead. He searched for it on Virus Total, an online repository where anyone can upload files to see if they\xe2\x80\x99re detected as malicious by different anti-viruses, and found it. \xe2\x80\x9cThis file matches one sample, and one sample only,\xe2\x80\x9d Marquis-Boire said during the talk. During our research we analyzed about 200 different examples of Adwind attacks covering the period November 2015-January 2016. We were able to identify about 60 different targets of these attacks and extract about 150\xc2 samples of Adwind (see related C2s and some hashes in the Appendix.) Most of the recipients fall into the category of financial organisations and manufacturing/engineering. We also found some government-(or -state) owned targets. It was reported that the email has come on behalf of\xc2 another bank located in Malaysia (faking the email \xe2\x80\x98From\xe2\x80\x99 field). The attacker is not an advanced threat actor as indicated by the habit of reusing the same email message template again and again, relying on a patched, three-year old MS Office vulnerability and commercially available malware tools such as the Adwind RAT. Yara signatures ...................................................................................... 81 mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 4TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com EXECUTIVE SUMMARY At the end of 2015 we became aware of an unusual malware program, discovered in an attempted attack on a bank in Singapore. Analysis of the file attached to a spear-phishing email that had been sent to the bank revealed the\xc2 name of the malware: JSocket. Later on we found that this malware has many names: Adwind RAT (Remote Access Tool), AlienSpy, Frutas, jFrutas, Unrecom, Sockrat, JSocket, jRat. The rich features of the malware, including its ability to run on Windows, Mac OS and Linux, as well as the fact that it was not detected by any antivirus solution meant that it immediately got our attention. Adwind is a backdoor available for purchase. It\xe2\x80\x99s written purely in Java which makes it cross-platform. The backdoor component (called the server) can\xc2 run on Windows, Mac OS, Linux and Android platforms, providing capabilities for remote desktop control, data gathering, data exfiltration and lateral movement. While it is more often used by opportunistic attackers and distributed in\xc2 massive spam campaigns, there are cases where Adwind has been used in\xc2 targeted attacks. In August 2015, Adwind popped up in the news in connection with a cyber-espionage campaign against an Argentinian prosecutor who had been found dead in January 2015. Currently the malware is distributed via a software-as-a-service platform which is based on an online subscription model. This report overviews the\xc2 capabilities of the malware, describes its online platform and lists the\xc2 cyber-attacks where this malware was used. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= http://motherboard.vice.com/read/malware-hunter-finds-spyware-used-against-dead-argentine-prosecutor 5TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com THE HISTORY OF ADWIND Frutas RAT The story begins in January 2012. The miscreant is definitely involved in targeted attacks with a major focus on financial institutions, using various techniques to reach the target. In September 2015, the attacker used spear-phishing emails with attached MS Word documents that exploited a patched vulnerability in Microsoft Office. In November of that year, the same attacker tried to hit the targets again using a Java backdoor. The attacker is not an advanced threat actor as indicated by the habit of reusing the same email message template again and again, relying on a patched, three-year old MS Office vulnerability and commercially available malware tools such as the Adwind RAT. Nevertheless, the threat coming from this actor has not yet been eradicated and his recurring attempts to attack various banks using new infection vectors are likely to continue, with the next attempt imminent. Despite several attempts to take down and stop the Adwind developers from distributing the malware, Adwind has survived for years and has been through rebranding and operational expansion that ranged from the provision of additional plugins for the malware to its own obfuscation tool and a even a warrant for FUD (fully undetected malware) to customers. The success of this commercial backdoor was so high that it inevitably led to the growth of malware resellers and copycats. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 60TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com While the concept of malware written in Java isn\xe2\x80\x99t new, the usage of multiple malware encryptors and obfuscators as well as unpacking in memory and a lack of full Java emulators (with the huge collection of classes that Java requires) in AV products makes this malware successful at passing through enterprise security fences. A simple infection vector based on an email with an attached JAR file is rather unique and unexpected. One of the reason why the attackers choose banks as targets may be the popularity of the Java platform in financial institutions as well as the attractive opportunity of a large-scale bank cyber -heist. The\xc2 malware depends on having Java runtime installed, which is more likely to be the case for enterprise users rather than typical home users. It is recommended that the Java platform is disabled or fully uninstalled from the system unless it is used. In case of a dependency on the Java platform it is recommended that modern and updated security software is used and that the\xc2 email filters are configured to block messages containing attached JAR files. mailto:intelreports%40kaspersky.com?subject= 61TLP: White For any inquiries, please contact intelreports@kaspersky.com For large organizations or users with basic experience, one simple trick may help to prevent accidental infection of the system with such JAR-based malware: changing the default handler for the JAR file extension. This can be achieved with two clicks in Windows or distributed via registry settings in a\xc2 large corporate network. Replacing the default JAR file handler application with, for instance, Windows Notepad will not only protect users from running malicious JARs but may also create enough confusion from encountering gibberish text to call the system administrator and bring a strange attachment to their attention. Adwind was and is an example of successful, widespread malware which runs on any platform. This malware set the bar for other malware writers who will most likely try to extend their support to other platforms in the future. The rich features of the malware, including its ability to run on Windows, Mac OS and Linux, as well as the fact that it was not detected by any antivirus solution meant that it immediately got our attention.

The backdoor component (called the server) can\xc2 run on Windows, Mac OS, Linux and Android platforms, providing capabilities for remote desktop control, data gathering, data exfiltration and lateral movement.

The miscreant is definitely involved in targeted attacks with a major focus on financial institutions, using various techniques to reach the target.

The attacker is not an advanced threat actor as indicated by the habit of reusing the same email message template again and again, relying on a patched, three-year old MS Office vulnerability and commercially available malware tools such as the Adwind RAT.

Nevertheless, the threat coming from this actor has not yet been eradicated and his recurring attempts to attack various banks using new infection vectors are likely to continue, with the next attempt imminent.

Despite several attempts to take down and stop the Adwind developers from distributing the malware, Adwind has survived for years and has been through rebranding and operational expansion that ranged from the provision of additional plugins for the malware to its own obfuscation tool and a even a warrant for FUD (fully undetected malware) to customers.
A simple infection vector based on an email with an attached JAR file is rather unique and unexpected.

One of the reason why the attackers choose banks as targets may be the popularity of the Java platform in financial institutions as well as the attractive opportunity of a large-scale bank cyber -heist.
The\xc2 malware depends on having Java runtime installed, which is more likely to be the case for enterprise users rather than typical home users.
It is recommended that the Java platform is disabled or fully uninstalled from the system unless it is used.

Replacing the default JAR file handler application with, for instance, Windows Notepad will not only protect users from running malicious JARs but may also create enough confusion from encountering gibberish text to call the system administrator and bring a strange attachment to their attention.
Adwind was and is an example of successful, widespread malware which runs on any platform.
This malware set the bar for other malware writers who will most likely try to extend their support to other platforms in the future.
As of January 2016, the website JSocket.org was still up and running.

In September 2015, the attacker used spear-phishing emails with attached MS Word documents that exploited a patched vulnerability in Microsoft Office.

A simple infection vector based on an email with an attached JAR file is rather unique and unexpected.

Adwind was and is an example of successful, widespread malware which runs on any platform.

The attacker is not an advanced threat actor as indicated by the habit of reusing the same email message template again and again, relying on a patched, three-year old MS Office vulnerability and commercially available malware tools such as the Adwind RAT.

Nevertheless, the threat coming from this actor has not yet been eradicated and his recurring attempts to attack various banks using new infection vectors are likely to continue, with the next attempt imminent.

Despite several attempts to take down and stop the Adwind developers from distributing the malware, Adwind has survived for years and has been through rebranding and operational expansion that ranged from the provision of additional plugins for the malware to its own obfuscation tool and a even a warrant for FUD (fully undetected malware) to customers.
A simple infection vector based on an email with an attached JAR file is rather unique and unexpected.

One of the reason why the attackers choose banks as targets may be the popularity of the Java platform in financial institutions as well as the attractive opportunity of a large-scale bank cyber -heist.
The\xc2 malware depends on having Java runtime installed, which is more likely to be the case for enterprise users rather than typical home users.
It is recommended that the Java platform is disabled or fully uninstalled from the system unless it is used.

Replacing the default JAR file handler application with, for instance, Windows Notepad will not only protect users from running malicious JARs but may also create enough confusion from encountering gibberish text to call the system administrator and bring a strange attachment to their attention.
Adwind was and is an example of successful, widespread malware which runs on any platform.
This malware set the bar for other malware writers who will most likely try to extend their support to other platforms in the future.
As of January 2016, the website JSocket.org was still up and running.
